introduction: Richard II's authority rests on inherited kingship, but his conduct turns family grievances and financial demands into a crisis of government. When a dispute between two nobles ends in banishment, its consequences reach beyond the men Richard sends away. His cousin Henry Bolingbroke returns to an England increasingly discontented with its ruler, while counsellors and relatives struggle to reconcile loyalty, law and survival. The struggle for the crown also becomes Richard's struggle to understand who he is when royal ceremony can no longer secure obedience.

fullSynopsis.text: Henry Bolingbroke accuses Thomas Mowbray of treason, including involvement in the Duke of Gloucester's murder. Richard II cannot reconcile them and authorizes trial by combat, but interrupts the contest before it begins. He banishes Mowbray for life and Bolingbroke for ten years, reduced to six out of regard for Bolingbroke's father, John of Gaunt. Gloucester's widow has meanwhile demanded vengeance from Gaunt, who believes Richard caused the murder but refuses to raise a hand against God's anointed king. Richard notices Bolingbroke's popularity with ordinary people and prepares expensive military action in Ireland.

Dying Gaunt denounces Richard's wasteful rule and the leasing of England's revenues. Richard dismisses the rebuke and, when Gaunt dies, seizes his property to finance the Irish war, depriving Bolingbroke of his inheritance. York warns that violating hereditary rights threatens the basis of Richard's own title. The king leaves York in charge and sails for Ireland. Northumberland, Ross and Willoughby join the returning Bolingbroke. The queen's forebodings become concrete news of rebellion, and Richard's favourites scatter. Bolingbroke tells York that he seeks only his lawful inheritance; unable to oppose him, York declares neutrality. Welsh forces disperse after rumours of Richard's death.

Bolingbroke condemns Bushy and Green to death for misleading Richard and injuring his own interests. Richard lands in Wales confident that divine kingship will protect him, but learns that his army has dispersed, Bushy, Green and Wiltshire are dead, and York has joined Bolingbroke. His declarations of sacred authority collapse into grief and reflections on the mortality of kings. At Flint Castle, Bolingbroke again demands restoration of his lands and an end to exile, backed by the threat of force. Richard grants the demands and goes with him towards London, recognizing that he can no longer determine his own course.

The queen overhears gardeners comparing the neglected kingdom to an unpruned garden and learns that Richard is in Bolingbroke's power. At Westminster, rival nobles renew accusations over Gloucester's death, especially against Aumerle; challenges accumulate without settling responsibility. York announces Richard's surrender of the crown to Bolingbroke. Carlisle protests that subjects cannot judge their king and predicts civil bloodshed, for which he is arrested. Richard is brought before the assembly and publicly gives up crown and sceptre. He resists reading a catalogue of offences, asks for a mirror and smashes it, distinguishing his visible performance of grief from the suffering within.

Bolingbroke arranges his coronation as Henry IV and sends Richard to confinement. Richard and the queen meet for a final farewell before he is taken to Pomfret and she is sent to France. A plot against Henry develops among Richard's supporters. York discovers his son Aumerle's written commitment to kill Henry at Oxford and rushes to expose him. Urged by his mother, Aumerle reaches the king first and begs forgiveness. York insists upon punishment, while the Duchess pleads for their son's life. Henry pardons Aumerle but orders action against the other conspirators. He also worries about his absent, dissolute son.

Exton interprets Henry's reported wish to be rid of a living fear as a request to kill Richard. In prison, Richard struggles to understand his lost identity and receives a loyal groom before Exton and armed servants attack. Richard kills two attackers but is struck down by Exton. At Windsor, Henry receives reports that the conspiracy has been crushed and several leaders beheaded; he allows Carlisle to live in retirement. Exton then presents Richard's coffin. Henry acknowledges having wished Richard dead but repudiates the murderer, denies him reward and sends him away. Mourning the death that stains his new power, Henry declares an intended pilgrimage to the Holy Land to seek cleansing.

acts.label: ACT I
acts.summary: Bolingbroke accuses Mowbray of treason and complicity in Gloucester's death. Both refuse Richard's attempts to reconcile them, and a judicial combat is arranged at Coventry. Gloucester's widow asks Gaunt to avenge her husband, but he attributes responsibility to Richard and leaves judgement to heaven rather than attacking an anointed king. Richard stops the combat before either man strikes and substitutes exile: Mowbray for life, Bolingbroke for ten years, then six. Gaunt cannot find comfort in that reduction, fearing he will die before his son returns. Richard observes Bolingbroke's popularity, plans new revenues to support his Irish campaign, and hopes to obtain the dying Gaunt's wealth.

acts.label: ACT II
acts.summary: Gaunt's last rebuke portrays Richard's government as a betrayal of England. After his death, Richard seizes his possessions despite York's warning that disinheriting Bolingbroke undermines lawful succession. Richard leaves for Ireland, making York governor. Discontented nobles join Bolingbroke, who returns in arms. The queen's apprehension deepens when news arrives of his landing and growing support. York struggles to gather resistance while the favourites separate: Bushy and Green seek Bristol, Bagot Ireland. Bolingbroke claims that he has returned only to recover Lancaster's inheritance. York condemns his rebellion but, lacking strength to arrest him, declares neutrality. In Wales, troops awaiting Richard disperse because they believe he is dead.

acts.label: ACT III
acts.summary: At Bristol, Bolingbroke sends Bushy and Green to execution. Richard returns from Ireland asserting that divine appointment guarantees his crown, but Salisbury and Scroop bring news of vanished military support, executions and widespread revolt. Richard vacillates between determination and despair, finally withdrawing to Flint Castle. Bolingbroke sends Northumberland to request restoration of his property and the repeal of banishment, threatening force if refused. Richard agrees and descends to meet him, aware that his freedom of action has gone. They depart for London. In York's garden, the queen overhears gardeners discussing Richard's capture and misgovernment; their knowledge of the political disaster precedes her own.

acts.label: ACT IV
acts.summary: At Westminster, Bagot accuses Aumerle of involvement in Gloucester's death. Other nobles challenge Aumerle and one another, but Bolingbroke postpones their disputes. Carlisle reports Mowbray's death abroad. York brings Richard's offer to surrender the throne, and Bolingbroke accepts it. Carlisle rejects the subjects' right to depose their king, foretells national bloodshed and is arrested. Summoned for a public resignation, Richard hands over the crown and verbally dismantles his authority. He refuses Northumberland's demand to read the charges against him and breaks a mirror that cannot display his inward grief. Bolingbroke sends him to the Tower and schedules his coronation. The Abbot, Carlisle and Aumerle remain to discuss a plot.

acts.label: ACT V
acts.summary: Richard and the queen exchange their final farewell as orders divide them between Pomfret and France. York discovers Aumerle's part in a conspiracy to kill Henry at Oxford. The Duchess sends her son ahead to beg pardon, then joins his plea against York's insistence on justice. Henry forgives him but pursues the other conspirators. Exton takes Henry's reported wish to lose his living fear as encouragement to kill Richard. At Pomfret, Richard reflects on kingship, time and imprisonment, speaks with a loyal groom, and dies fighting his attackers. Henry hears of the rebellion's defeat and spares Carlisle. Presented with Richard's coffin, he condemns Exton and announces a penitential pilgrimage.
